name: Proof of Work
tagline: Security purchased with electricity and computational effort.
overview: Validators (miners) compete to solve a computationally expensive cryptographic puzzle. The first to solve it proposes the next block and earns the block reward.
mechanism: Miners repeatedly hash block data with a changing nonce until the output falls below a target difficulty. Solving the puzzle is hard; verifying the solution is trivial for every other node.
advantages: Battle-tested security over 15+ years
No prior token stake required to participate
Highly resistant to Sybil attacks via real-world hardware cost
disadvantages: Very high energy consumption
Slow finality and low throughput
Mining pool centralization risk
workflow: Nodes broadcast pending transactions to the mempool
Miners assemble a candidate block from pending transactions
Miners iterate a nonce searching for a hash below the difficulty target
First valid solution is broadcast to the network
Peers verify the solution and extend their chain
Block reward and fees are paid to the winning miner

security.attack51: High cost, requires majority hash power

name: Proof of Stake
tagline: Security backed by locked capital, replacing energy with collateral.
overview: Validators lock up (stake) native tokens as collateral. The protocol selects a validator to propose each block, weighted by stake size.
mechanism: A pseudo-random algorithm selects a validator proportional to their stake. Validators who act maliciously have a portion of their stake destroyed (slashed).
advantages: Dramatically lower energy consumption than PoW (~99.9% reduction)
Faster block times and higher throughput
Economic penalties (slashing) discourage misbehavior
disadvantages: Wealth concentration can influence validator selection
Nothing-at-stake theoretical concerns
Complex slashing and unbonding logic
workflow: Validators lock native tokens into a staking contract
Protocol pseudo-randomly selects a block proposer by stake weight
Proposer builds and broadcasts a candidate block
Other validators attest to the block's validity
Block finalizes once attestation quorum is reached
Rewards distributed; malicious behavior is slashed

name: Proof of Authority
tagline: Identity-vetted validators, tuned for enterprise and private chains.
overview: A small set of pre-approved, identity-verified validators take turns producing blocks, prioritizing speed and predictability over full decentralization.
mechanism: Validators are whitelisted based on verified identity and real-world reputation. They sign blocks in a known rotation; misbehavior damages their public identity.
advantages: Extremely fast and predictable block times
Minimal computational and energy overhead
Ideal for consortium and private enterprise networks
disadvantages: Highly centralized validator set
Requires trust in real-world validator identities
Not fully censorship resistant
workflow: A governing body approves and whitelists validator identities
Validators are assigned a deterministic signing rotation
The scheduled validator signs and broadcasts the next block
Other authorities verify the signature and identity
Chain extends immediately with high confidence
Misbehaving authorities can be removed by governance vote

name: Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance
tagline: State machine replication with multi-round voting guarantees.
overview: A known set of nodes exchange multiple rounds of signed messages to reach agreement, tolerating up to one-third faulty or malicious nodes.
mechanism: A leader proposes a value; nodes broadcast pre-prepare, prepare, and commit messages until two-thirds agree, achieving immediate finality.
advantages: Instant, deterministic finality with zero chain forks
No block rollback possibility once committed
Well-understood formal mathematical guarantees
disadvantages: Communication overhead scales quadratically with node count O(n²)
Impractical for massive open validator sets
Requires permissioned/known participant pool
workflow: A leader node proposes a candidate block (pre-prepare)
Nodes broadcast 'prepare' messages to all peers
Nodes wait for 2f+1 matching prepare messages
Nodes broadcast 'commit' messages once prepared
Block commits once 2f+1 commit messages are collected
Result is final immediately with no possibility of reorg

name: Avalanche Consensus
tagline: Agreement by repeated sub-sampling, avoiding global broadcasts.
overview: Nodes repeatedly query small random subsets of peers and adopt the majority preference, rapidly converging on consensus probabilistically.
mechanism: Each node queries k random validators about a transaction; if a strong majority agrees, confidence increases. Repeated sub-sampling rounds converge to finality in sub-seconds.
advantages: Sub-second finality at large validator scale
High throughput without O(n²) communication complexity
Thousands of validators can participate without network slowdown
disadvantages: Newer design with shorter historical security track record
Probabilistic safety model rather than traditional BFT lockouts
More complex to reason about mathematically
workflow: A node receives a new transaction and forms an initial preference
The node queries k randomly sampled validators for their preference
If a supermajority agrees, the node's confidence increases
The sampling round repeats with new random subsets
Confidence accumulates until a finality threshold is crossed
Transaction is accepted as final across the network

name: Proof of History
tagline: A cryptographic time-recorder that orders transactions before voting.
overview: A verifiable delay function generates a sequential hash chain proving elapsed time, letting nodes agree on ordering before consensus runs.
mechanism: A leader continuously hashes its output in a single thread. Incoming transactions are stamped into this hash sequence, providing indisputable cryptographic ordering.
advantages: Eliminates network overhead of negotiating transaction timestamps
Enables ultra-high real-world throughput and fast block times
Pairs seamlessly with stake-weighted voting layers
disadvantages: Requires high-end single-core CPU hardware to maintain hash chain
Prone to network congestion during spike loads
Relies on scheduled sequential leader rotation
workflow: The current leader continuously hashes its own prior output
Transactions are timestamped by insertion into the hash sequence
The sequence is broadcast as a verifiable proof of elapsed time
Validators replay the hash chain to confirm ordering
A stake-weighted voting layer finalizes the ordered blocks
Leadership rotates on a fixed schedule

name: Proof of Capacity
tagline: Trading hard drive storage space for computational energy.
overview: Also known as Proof of Space, participants pre-compute and store data plots on disk. Block creation rights go to whoever holds a matching plot closest to a target challenge.
mechanism: Miners 'plot' hard drives with precomputed cryptographic hashes once. When a challenge is issued, miners read local plots to find the closest solution.
advantages: Far lower energy use than ASIC computation (uses idle drive power)
Recycles standard consumer and enterprise storage hardware
ASIC-resistant distribution model
disadvantages: Initial plotting phase is slow and disk-wear intensive
Arm-race toward purchasing massive storage arrays
Smaller developer ecosystem compared to PoW/PoS
workflow: Miners generate large plot files of precomputed hashes
Plots are stored permanently on local hard disks
The network issues a random challenge every block
Miners scan their local plots for the closest matching value
The closest match wins the right to produce the next block
Block is broadcast and verified by peer nodes

name: Proof of Burn
tagline: Destroying real token value to earn permanent virtual mining power.
overview: Participants send native tokens to a verifiably unspendable eater address, 'burning' them. The protocol grants virtual mining power proportional to the burned value.
mechanism: Coins are sent to an unspendable burn address (no private key exists). The protocol treats destroyed coins as long-term financial commitment, granting block proposal rights.
advantages: Zero ongoing hardware or electrical costs after burning
Deflationary tokenomics that benefit all token holders
Allows bootstrapping new chains using established assets (e.g. BTC)
disadvantages: Permanently destroys capital (economically irreversible)
Favors early wealthy participants with initial capital
Virtual mining power requires decay mechanisms to prevent monopoly
workflow: A participant sends tokens to an unspendable eater address
The burn transaction is recorded permanently on-chain
The protocol calculates virtual mining power from burned value
Burned power decays gradually over time, encouraging fresh burns
Participants with highest active virtual power win block rights
New blocks are broadcast and verified by network peers
